extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of combustion turbine EGUs, power-sector stakeholders, regulators, and environmental policy commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of regulatory criteria and standards used by EPA to subcategorize stationary combustion turbines (low/intermediate/base load), determine electric-sales thresholds, define system emergencies, and identify the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and associated performance standards for new and reconstructed combustion turbines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales thresholds for combustion turbine subcategories
rubrics_metrics.description: 12-operating month electric sales thresholds for subcategories of combustion turbine EGUs: Low Load ≤20 percent, Intermediate Load >20 and ≤40 percent, Base Load >40 percent (percent of potential electric sales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 summarizes the thresholds. These thresholds distinguish between low, intermediate, and base load turbines for purposes of applying appropriate standards of performance and BSERs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low Load Subcategory — definition and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Low load subcategory includes combustion turbines that operate only during periods of peak electric demand (i.e., peaking units). Low load turbines also provide ramping capability and other ancillary services and generally operate for short periods and potentially at relatively low duty cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This type of operation reduces efficiency and increases emission rates regardless of design efficiency or maintenance, making it difficult to establish a reasonable output-based standard of performance for low load combustion turbines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low load electric sales threshold (final: 20 percent)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing a fixed low load electric sales threshold of 20 percent of potential electric sales to distinguish low load from intermediate load subcategories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluated thresholds of 10, 15, 20, and 25 percent. 10 percent was problematic (highly variable emission rates; would bring most new simple cycle turbines into intermediate load). At >15 percent many GHG emission rates begin to stabilize; >20 percent emission rates clearly stabilize for most simple cycle turbines. The fixed 20 percent represents a utilization level where most simple cycle turbines perform consistently, enabling an output-based BSER for higher-utilization subcategories. EPA solicited comments on a 15–25% range and a sliding-scale alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate Load Subcategory — definition and BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediate load combustion turbines are those selling greater than 20 percent and up to 40 percent of potential electric output. The final BSER for the intermediate load subcategory is highly efficient simple cycle generation (plus efficient operation and maintenance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed sliding-scale approach had different thresholds for simple cycle vs combined cycle, and a multi-component BSER (including potential hydrogen co-firing phases) was proposed; EPA is not finalizing a second BSER component or phase-2 standard for intermediate load turbines at this time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base Load Subcategory — definition and BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Base load combustion turbines are those selling more than 40 percent of potential electric output. The first-component BSER is highly efficient combined cycle generation; the second-component BSER (phase-2) is highly efficient combined cycle generation plus 90 percent CCS (beginning in 2032).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners/operators of new/reconstructed base load turbines must meet phase-1 standards based on efficient combined-cycle generation upon startup, and meet phase-2 standards (including 90% CCS) for 12-operating-month rolling averages that begin on or after January 2032.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER selection and phased approach
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluated multiple BSER components: combusting lower-emitting fuels, using highly efficient generation, using CCS, and co-firing with low-GHG hydrogen; EPA proposed multi-component BSERs with phased standards of performance to allow time for infrastructure development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For intermediate and base load subcategories EPA proposed phased standards (initial efficient generation, later hydrogen co-firing or CCS). For base load EPA finalized a CCS pathway; EPA did not finalize hydrogen co-firing as a BSER component for intermediate or base load at this time. EPA solicited comment on alternate phasing and timeframes and on whether hydrogen co-firing should be a compliance pathway to an overall CCS-based standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of integrated onsite renewable generation
rubrics_metrics.description: The rated output of integrated renewables is included when determining the design efficiency of the affected facility and is included in determining the emissions rate of the affected facility, but the output of integrated renewables is not included when determining the net electric sales for subcategorization applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including integrated renewables in design efficiency increases allowable potential electric sales (thus increases operational flexibility). EPA reasoned that including integrated renewables in subcategorization could discourage their use or lead to moving into a more stringent subcategory; estimated effect on emissions rate is approximately a 1 percent lowering when renewables are considered for emissions rate calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of integrated energy storage
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated output of energy storage is included when determining the design efficiency of the affected facility, but the output from energy storage is not considered in determining the NSPS emissions rate nor as net electric sales for subcategorization applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Energy storage increases flexibility and would likely reduce capacity factors for associated simple cycle turbines, but because storage may be charged with higher-emitting generation the EPA is not including storage output in emissions rate or subcategorization calculations at this time; EPA may further evaluate impacts in future rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: System emergency — exclusion of generation from net electric sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Electricity sold during hours of operation when a unit is called upon due to a system emergency is not counted toward the percentage electric sales subcategorization threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exclusion provides flexibility to maintain system reliability. EPA is including the system emergency concept in subpart TTTTa and clarifying determination and documentation of emergencies; local grid operator (balancing authority or reliability coordinator) will determine EGUs essential to maintaining grid reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of system emergency — inclusion/exclusion of EEA levels
rubrics_metrics.description: System emergency is defined to include Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) levels 2 and 3 but not EEA level 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EEA levels 2 and 3 correspond to time-limited, well-defined, and relatively infrequent energy-deficiency situations; EPA excluded EEA level 1 because such events are often preparatory, more frequent, longer in duration, and their inclusion would risk increasing overall GHG emissions without meaningful reliability benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate standard of performance during system emergencies for units with CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: During system emergencies, owners/operators of EGUs equipped with CCS may temporarily reduce the capture rate or cease capture and, in place of the applicable output-based emissions standard, would be subject to a BSER based on the combustion of lower-emitting fuels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emissions and output during system emergency hours would not be included when calculating the 12-operating-month emissions rate. EPA rejected an alternate emissions standard based on efficient generation for emergencies because (a) emergencies are limited and not representative of achievable long-term rates, (b) EGUs with CCS may not operate efficiently without CCS, and (c) costs/time to start/stop CCS are high and could encourage operational anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE section 202(c) orders — compliance protection
rubrics_metrics.description: An affected source operating pursuant to a DOE section 202(c) order (temporary generation ordered for emergencies) is deemed not to be operating in violation of its environmental requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such orders may be issued for 90 days and extended in 90-day increments after consultation with EPA; DOE has historically issued them at the request of generators/RTOs to enable supply during expected emergency-related generation shortfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-fuel-fired combustion turbine treatment and heat-input standard
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is not including a separate multi-fuel subcategory for low/intermediate/base load turbines in the new rule; multi-fuel-fired turbines commencing construction or reconstruction after May 23, 2023 will be placed in subcategories based on electric sales. Performance standards for each subcategory will be adjusted for multi-fuel-fired turbines to reflect higher GHG emission rates of some fuels, with a maximum allowable heat-input-based emissions rate of 160 lb CO2/MMBtu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids circumvention where owners/operators burn ≥10% non-natural gas fuels to remain in a less stringent multi-fuel subcategory. Adjusted standards ensure BSER (efficient generation) is applied while accounting for higher-emitting fuels; e.g., fuel-oil fired turbine standard could be ~33% higher than natural gas basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-load BSER and associated heat-input standard history
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent with the 2015 NSPS, the BSER for the low load subcategory is the use of lower-emitting fuels; historically the 2015 NSPS applied a heat-input-based standard of 120 lb CO2/MMBtu for newly constructed/reconstructed non-base load natural gas-fired turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA concluded efficient design/operation could not reasonably be applied as BSER for low-load units due to variability in operation (multiple starts/stops) and the difficulty of defining a uniform output-based standard; hence a heat-input-based, lower-emitting-fuels approach was appropriate despite limited GHG reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sliding-scale electric sales threshold alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA solicited comment on a sliding-scale threshold based on a percentage of design efficiency (three-fourths of design efficiency), which would vary the electric sales threshold depending on turbine design efficiency (e.g., simple cycle turbines selling less than 18–22% depending on design efficiency would be low load).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach mirrors an approach used in the 2015 NSPS to recognize environmental benefit of more efficient turbines; EPA considered but finalized a fixed 20% threshold after comments supported both lower and higher thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical basis — capacity factor at which emission rates stabilize
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA used hourly emissions data and observed that GHG emission rates for many simple cycle turbines begin to stabilize above a capacity factor of 15 percent and clearly stabilize for most turbines above 20 percent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA reported that half of recently constructed simple cycle turbines have maintained 12-operating month capacity factors of 15% or less, two-thirds ≤20%, and ~80% ≤25%. This empirical stability informed the selection of the 20% low-load threshold and rejection of 10%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision not to create rural/small utility subcategory
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA determined that a subcategory for rural electric cooperatives and small utility distribution systems (serving 50,000 customers or less) is not appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments suggested BSERs involving hydrogen co-firing or CCS could impose hardship on disadvantaged communities and small entities; EPA concluded BSER for new turbines does not include hydrogen co-firing and CCS qualifies as BSER for base load nationwide, therefore a separate rural/small-utility subcategory is not warranted.
